rows.subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
rows.description: A child stamps feet or storms off after losing an argument. It shows intense feeling and a need to leave; teaching a cooling-off routine, such as walking then returning to talk, turns the impulse into a safe boundary.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child wraps arms around the body or a soft toy after upset or during a scary film. Self-hugging is a gentle way to soothe; it may also hint at cold or worry, so a quiet check-in is more useful than assuming.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A schoolchild recognises when a peer shrinks, ducks or covers the face during a taunt. It may signal fear or pain rather than weakness; the wise response is to stop, help and tell a teacher, not to keep going.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
rows.description: A schoolchild sees a peer scratch the head or rub the forehead during a test and may guess confusion. It may instead be an itch or tiredness; a friendly are you stuck offer beats assuming.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A schoolchild twirls hair, tugs a sleeve or straightens a uniform when nervous or self-conscious. These are common self-comfort acts, and observers should not read them as lying or flirting; they only show mild tension.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child in some cultures walks with friends hand in hand or gets a pat on the back from a teacher. Meaning is friendship or reassurance, not romance; children should learn that any touch that makes them uncomfortable can be refused and reported.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A schoolchild uses a high-five to celebrate, a fist bump for friendly greeting or a handshake to be polite. These quick touches show warmth and respect, and a child who prefers not to touch can offer a wave instead.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A schoolchild notices a friend moving to another table or turning away after an argument. It may signal hurt or anger, but could also mean need for space; a kind note or an invitation later repairs more than pushing.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Leaning closer to share and secrets [Expressing]
rows.description: A child leans in to whisper, share a joke or show a phone screen. It signals trust and inclusion; those left out may feel excluded, so including others or being kind when sharing is wise.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A schoolchild learns to tell friendly laughter from laughter that mocks. Warm laughter includes the person and fits the mood, while laughing at someone's mistake or difference can hurt; joining in a joke at another's expense should be avoided.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
